summary: This informational document is a source of information about the Russian federal standard hash function GOST R 34.11-2012, one of the Russian cryptographic standard algorithms. It updates RFC 5831.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6986 describes a hash function in the Russian GOST R 34.11-2012 standard. The function turns a message into a fixed-length result used by cryptographic systems.

questions: how long is the gost hash code
subtitle: The Russian GOST R 34.11-2012 hash algorithm and its two output lengths.

tldr.problem: Developers needed an English-language description of the Russian Federal hash standard GOST R 34.11-2012.
tldr.mechanism: The algorithm processes messages in 512-bit blocks with a round function and final length and checksum steps, producing a 512-bit or 256-bit hash code.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6986 is an Informational description that updates RFC 5831. The RFC says GOST R 34.11-2012 superseded GOST R 34.11-94 from 1 January 2013.

today: RFC 6986 is an Informational document published in August 2013 and updates RFC 5831. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that later updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope of the Hash Standard
sections.content:
GOST R 34.11-2012 defines a hash function and a procedure for calculating it from a binary message. The RFC records the Russian Federal standard for use in cryptographic methods, including integrity, authenticity and digital-signature processes.

The standard was developed with participation from InfoTeCS JSC and approved by Decree #216 in 2012. RFC 6986 says it updates RFC 5831 and describes itself as an independent informational submission.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes one standard method for calculating a hash from a message. A hash is a fixed-length result that cryptographic processes can use when checking data.

sections.title: Transition from the Earlier Standard
sections.content:
The RFC states that GOST R 34.11-2012 superseded GOST R 34.11-94 on 1 January 2013. New systems submitted for certification MUST use the 2012 function and MAY also use the earlier function for compatibility with existing systems.

The text allows use of GOST R 34.11-94 in current systems for at least a five-year period. This transition rule is part of the national standard described by the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard replaced an earlier hash function. New systems submitted for certification must use the new function, but may also support the old one for compatibility.

sections.title: Message and Hash Sizes
sections.content:
The standard defines two hash-code lengths: 512 bits and 256 bits. Both functions accept a message shorter than 2^512 bits and process its contents in 512-bit blocks.

The 512-bit variant starts from an all-zero 512-bit value. The 256-bit variant starts from the byte pattern (00000001)^64; after the final calculation, it keeps the 256 most significant bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm offers two result lengths: 512 bits and 256 bits. Both process the message in 512-bit blocks, but they use different starting values.

sections.title: Transforming Blocks into a Hash
sections.content:
The algorithm uses four transformations on 512-bit values: XOR with a value, byte substitution, byte permutation and a linear transformation. These operations form the LPS transformation used in the round function.

The calculation updates a running hash for each complete message block and tracks the processed length and a checksum. It pads the last incomplete block, then applies two final rounds using the length and checksum to produce the hash code.
sections.plainLanguage: The function repeatedly changes each message block and combines it with a running result. At the end, it includes the message length and accumulated checksum in the final calculation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section consists of the statement that the document as a whole concerns security. It does not provide a separate analysis of the algorithm's strength.

Elsewhere, the RFC defines a collision-resistant hash by properties involving the difficulty of finding an input for an output, a second matching input, or any two distinct inputs with the same output.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not assess the algorithm's security strength in detail. It defines collision resistance as making several kinds of matching-input searches computationally infeasible.
